addressed_problems.content: The paper provides empirical evidence that magnitude-based pruning (iterative magnitude pruning and one-shot global pruning) can identify highly sparse winning tickets in PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN architectures while maintaining classification accuracy on 3D point cloud datasets such as ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN. However, a formal theoretical proof explaining why such lottery-ticket-style sparse subnetworks exist specifically for Point Cloud Neural Networks (PCNNs) is missing. It remains unresolved how the pruning process preserves geometric invariances (e.g., rotations, scaling) and structural constraints (e.g., part relationships, symmetry) that are critical for 3D shape understanding. Without this theoretical foundation, the generalizability and reliability of the observed pruning phenomenon across different PCNN architectures and geometric transformations cannot be guaranteed, limiting the ability to design principled pruning strategies for 3D point cloud models.

The paper hypothesizes that preserving the highest-magnitude weights through pruning maintains geometric invariances and structural semantics of 3D shapes, and shows empirically that pruned networks achieve comparable accuracy on rotated and scaled point clouds. However, the exact degree to which pruning preserves these invariances and structural constraints has not been formally proven or quantified. Beyond empirical robustness, there are no theoretical guarantees or formal metrics that characterize the preservation of rotation invariance, scaling invariance, or inter-part relationships after extreme pruning (e.g., 99% sparsity). This gap prevents a rigorous understanding of when and why pruning succeeds or fails for geometrically complex 3D data, and limits the development of pruning methods with guaranteed invariance properties.

The identification of winning tickets in PCNNs via iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) requires multiple train-prune-rewind cycles—up to 100 cycles for PointNet and 80 cycles for DGCNN and PointCNN—making the process computationally expensive for each new task or dataset. While one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity achieves comparable results, the overall cost of discovering effective sparse subnetworks remains high. The development or validation of cheaper, single-pass, or more efficient pruning algorithms that are specifically tailored to the high-dimensional and geometrically complex nature of 3D point cloud models is an open engineering challenge. Addressing this gap is essential for practical deployment where computational resources for repeated training are limited.

The paper demonstrates that winning tickets discovered on the large synthetic ShapeNetCore dataset can be transferred to smaller datasets (ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN) while maintaining competitive accuracy—for example, 86.3% on ModelNet40 with 99% sparse PointNet. However, the accuracy drop is more pronounced when transferring to the real-world scanned dataset ScanObjectNN (e.g., from 68.2% base to 64.7% with IMP at 99% sparsity) compared to synthetic-to-synthetic transfers. This indicates that the limits of ticket transferability across domain shifts—such as from clean synthetic data to noisy real-world scans—remain poorly understood. It is an open question how to characterize and improve the robustness of transferred sparse subnetworks under domain gaps, including variations in point density, noise, and partial occlusions present in real-world 3D data.

The paper achieves extreme unstructured sparsity (up to 99%) in PCNNs by pruning individual weights, resulting in models with far fewer parameters (e.g., 0.034M for PointNet at 99% sparsity). However, unstructured sparsity does not automatically translate to proportional reductions in inference latency, energy consumption, or memory bandwidth on conventional hardware (GPUs, CPUs) or edge accelerators, which often rely on dense matrix operations or structured sparsity for speedup. Quantifying the actual runtime, energy, and memory benefits of these extremely sparse PCNN subnetworks on target deployment platforms—especially resource-constrained edge devices—remains an open empirical question. Without such measurements, the practical value of the discovered winning tickets for real-time autonomous systems or 3D computer vision applications cannot be fully assessed.

The processing of 3D point clouds with deep neural networks (Point Cloud Neural Networks, PCNNs) faces a concrete pre-existing scientific problem: modern PCNNs must capture complex, high-dimensional geometric structure (permutation invariance, rotations/scalings, and structural part relationships) and therefore have grown highly overparameterized, which increases latency, memory use, and energy consumption and impedes deployment in resource-constrained settings. Prior compression and efficiency approaches for 3D data (quantization, channel pruning, sparsity regularization, knowledge distillation, and specially designed compact architectures) either rely on structured reductions that limit architectural choices or have not been shown to remove the large unstructured redundancy present in overparameterized 3D models. In particular, the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) and unstructured magnitude-based pruning techniques — which in 2D tasks have revealed trainable sparse subnetworks — were not previously explored or validated for PCNNs. This gap is compounded by domain-specific obstacles: (1) geometric complexity and invariance requirements of 3D shapes mean that pruning may destroy symmetry- or transformation-sensitive features unless critical weights are preserved; (2) the irregular, high-dimensional nature of point clouds tends to require more parameters to represent spatial relationships, making it unclear whether sparse subnetworks can retain accuracy; and (3) structural constraints among parts of 3D objects create the risk that naive pruning breaks semantic or geometric integrity. Because of these limitations, researchers lacked a demonstrated procedure and empirical evidence showing whether unstructured magnitude pruning (including one-shot global pruning and Iterative Magnitude Pruning) can (a) discover sparse, trainable subnetworks in standard PCNNs that match dense-model accuracy, (b) do so without violating geometric/structural constraints relevant to 3D classification, and (c) produce subnetworks that transfer across related 3D tasks — all while being computationally feasible to obtain and useful for deployment. This work is therefore necessary to establish whether the LTH-style pruning paradigm meaningfully reduces PCNN size and computational cost without unacceptable degradation of 3D classification performance and to identify which pruning strategies and layer types are critical to preserve.

nodes.content: In 3D shape classification, practitioners need compact models that retain accuracy for deployment, but existing dense PCNNs have millions of parameters because of the need to represent irregular, high-dimensional point-cloud geometry. Prior art provided limited evidence that unstructured pruning or LTH-style subnetworks exist and are trainable for PCNNs; without such evidence it was unclear whether magnitude-based pruning would catastrophically remove weights encoding geometric invariances or produce subnetworks that fail to train to competitive accuracy. This uncertainty prevented adoption of aggressive unstructured pruning for PCNN compression and left open whether extreme sparsification (e.g., 99% removal of weights) is feasible without substantial accuracy loss.

To compress PCNNs while preserving geometric and structural features it is necessary to choose a pruning criterion and schedule. Prior pruning schemes included local layer-wise magnitude thresholds and iterative schedules tuned for 2D CNNs, but these approaches may fail on PCNNs because important weights appear distributed across layers and because local thresholds can remove globally-critical weights. Without an empirically validated strategy, practitioners could apply pruning that either fails to achieve extreme sparsity or causes larger-than-acceptable accuracy drops. Establishing which pruning regime (global one-shot versus iterative local) reliably finds sparse, trainable subnetworks for 3D models is therefore essential to make unstructured pruning practicable for PCNN compression.

In 3D classification, datasets often differ in size and domain (synthetic versus real scans), and training separate overparameterized models and performing expensive pruning for every target dataset is computationally burdensome. In the 2D domain, LTH has shown cross-dataset transferability, but for 3D point clouds this property was unverified: without empirical evidence, researchers could not rely on a single discovered sparse subnetwork to serve multiple 3D tasks, nor could they assess whether such transfer would preserve geometric features or accuracy. Demonstrating transferability would permit reusing sparse models discovered on large datasets to accelerate training and deployment for smaller or related 3D datasets.

To design compact PCNN architectures or to target layerwise pruning schedules for hardware-efficient deployment, researchers need to know which parts of the network encode essential geometric representations. Prior to this work, it was unclear whether conv layers or FC layers carried the majority of critical information in PCNNs; without that insight, pruning could remove essential conv filters or leave large FC parameter blocks intact, resulting in poor trade-offs between size and accuracy. A layerwise understanding is required to guide focused compression (e.g., eliminating FC parameters) while preserving the conv layers that extract geometric features.

Practitioners aiming for very small 3D models have a choice between designing inherently compact architectures or pruning large models. Before this study, there was limited empirical evidence that unstructured pruning of large PCNNs could produce parameter budgets smaller than carefully engineered compact networks while maintaining acceptable accuracy. Without this evidence, the community lacked guidance on whether to invest effort in new compact architectures or to rely on aggressive pruning of existing overparameterized models to reach extreme parameter reductions.

Point Cloud Neural Networks (PCNNs) – specifically PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN – contain sparse subnetworks obtained by magnitude-based pruning. When only the top 1% of weights by magnitude are retained (99% sparsity), these subnetworks achieve test accuracies on the ModelNet40 dataset that are close to the unpruned baselines. For instance, after discovering subnetworks on the ShapeNetCore dataset via global Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) or one-shot global pruning and then transferring them to ModelNet40, the accuracies are: PointNet baseline 87.5% compared to 86.3% (IMP) and 86.9% (one-shot); DGCNN baseline 89.2% compared to 88.5% (IMP) and 88.0% (one-shot); PointCNN baseline 90.2% compared to 87.4% (IMP) and 86.9% (one-shot). These results demonstrate that retaining only the top 1% highest-magnitude weights can preserve the majority of classification performance on ModelNet40 for these PCNN architectures.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that PCNNs contain highly sparse subnetworks with near-baseline accuracy draws its strongest support from the direct ablation on PointNet (H2) and the consistent pattern across three diverse architectures (H1). However, three load-bearing uncertainties remain: (P1) the pruning procedure lacks LTH's rewinding step, so the subnetworks are not proven to be winning tickets trainable from scratch, which undermines the claimed LTH interpretation; (P2) all reported accuracies come from single runs without error bars, making the quantitative gaps to baseline (0.7–2.8 points) unanchored against run-to-run variability; (P3) the large accuracy drops on the real-world ScanObjectNN benchmark (3.5–11.1 points at 99% sparsity) show that the "near-baseline" property does not generalize to real data, materially narrowing the conclusion's valid scope. The highlights (H1, H2) underwrite the existence claim for synthetic data and for PointNet in particular, and they provide a structural breadth that partially offsets the limited architecture coverage in the ablation (only PointNet). Nonetheless, the unprotected risks on statistical reliability (P2) and domain generalization (P3) mean the conclusion's quantitative claim is credible only for synthetic benchmarks and must be qualified by the absence of multi-run verification. The LTH framing (P1) is a separate conceptual risk that does not affect the numerical existence evidence but does challenge the paper's central theoretical attribution.

nodes.title: Existence of highly sparse, trainable subnetworks (winning tickets) in PCNNs up to 99% sparsity with near-baseline accuracy on ModelNet40

nodes.content: Global magnitude pruning executed as a one-shot operation (a single pruning cycle, J=1) or as global Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) identifies winning-ticket subnetworks at extreme sparsity levels (99%) on the ModelNet40 3D shape classification dataset more reliably than iterative layer-local pruning. In particular, one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity achieves higher test accuracy than both iterative local pruning and global IMP across the PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN network architectures.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that global pruning (one-shot or IMP) outperforms local pruning for PCNNs is supported by a mechanistic cross-validation (H3) that explains why global pruning naturally preserves critical conv layers. This highlight partially addresses the concern (P5) that local pruning may be disadvantaged by its equal-per-layer ratio, but it does not fully close the gap because H3 is based on PointNet ablation, and the local vs global comparison in Figure 2 includes DGCNN and PointCNN without separate layerwise ablations. The claim that one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity "exceeds all other methods" faces severe evidentiary weakness: P4 documents the absence of any run-to-run error bands on the comparison curves, P5 documents the likely unfairness of the local pruning implementation, and P6 documents that the surprising result of one-shot beating iterative IMP goes unexplained and likely reflects a suboptimal IMP schedule rather than a general truth. The highlights (H3) are insufficient to offset the combination of P4, P5, and P6: the comparative ranking is not statistically anchored (P4), the key comparison may be biased (P5), and the most striking sub-claim (one-shot > IMP) is mechanistically improbable without further evidence (P6). The conclusion's reliability is therefore moderate, and a practitioner should not treat the global-strategy superiority as a settled design rule without additional controlled experiments.

nodes.title: Global one-shot magnitude pruning outperforms iterative local pruning and global IMP at extreme sparsity for PCNNs

nodes.content: Sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) discovered on the ShapeNetCore 3D dataset transfer to the ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN datasets while retaining comparable or acceptable accuracy after fine-tuning. For subnetworks at 60% sparsity transferred to ModelNet40: PointNet achieves 88.2% (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP) and 87.8% (one-shot global pruning) vs. dense baseline 87.5%; DGCNN achieves 90.1% (IMP) and 90.4% (one-shot) vs. baseline 89.2%; PointCNN achieves 90.6% (IMP) and 90.4% (one-shot) vs. baseline 90.2%. For the same 60% sparsity transferred to ScanObjectNN: PointNet achieves 71.7% (IMP) and 70.5% (one-shot) vs. baseline 68.2%; DGCNN achieves 75.2% (IMP) and 74.9% (one-shot) vs. baseline 71.1%; PointCNN achieves 73.2% (IMP) and 72.9% (one-shot) vs. baseline 70.4%. At 99% sparsity, transferred accuracies on ModelNet40 remain close to baselines (e.g., PointNet IMP 86.3% vs. 87.5%; DGCNN IMP 88.5% vs. 89.2%; PointCNN IMP 87.4% vs. 90.2%), while on ScanObjectNN the drops are larger (e.g., PointNet IMP 64.7% vs. 68.2%; DGCNN IMP 64.6% vs. 71.1%; PointCNN IMP 65.3% vs. 70.4%). These results indicate that winning tickets discovered on one 3D domain can be reused to reduce training and parameter costs on related 3D classification tasks.

metadata.narrative: The transferability conclusion is partially supported: H4 shows successful transfer at 60% sparsity across both synthetic and real datasets, which is a genuine empirical contribution. However, the claim as stated is unqualified with respect to sparsity level and domain, and P7 directly shows that at 99% sparsity on real-world ScanObjectNN, accuracy drops are large and likely unacceptable, contradicting the unqualified claim. P8 shows that the experimental design cannot distinguish transferability due to the sparsity pattern from transferability due to standard pre-training, because no dense-transfer baseline is included. P9 further limits the scope to one source dataset. The interaction between these premises is compounding: P7 shows that the claim fails at the sparsity level emphasized in the paper, P8 shows that even the 60% success might be due to pre-training rather than sparsity, and P9 shows the generalization space is narrow. H4 is an important empirical demonstration but it does not offset P8 or P9, and it is partially contradicted by P7 (the 60% success on real data does not extend to 99%). The overall reliability is low: the conclusion's unqualified form is unsupported, and even a qualified version (≤60% sparsity, synthetic source) faces the confound issue (P8). The paper does not resolve whether the sparsity pattern or the pre-training is responsible for the observed transfer outcomes.

nodes.title: Transferability of winning-ticket subnetworks across 3D datasets from ShapeNetCore to ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN

nodes.content: Layerwise analysis of Point Cloud Neural Networks (PCNNs) after magnitude pruning shows that convolutional layers retain a disproportionately large fraction of high-magnitude, task-critical weights, while fully-connected (FC) layers contribute most of the removable parameters. In an ablation on the PointNet architecture (a specific PCNN) using the ModelNet40 dataset, pruning only FC layer weights at a 99% pruning rate (i.e., removing 99% of FC weights) yields an overall network sparsity of 87% and a test accuracy of 88.3%, which exceeds the unpruned baseline accuracy of 87.5%. Pruning only convolutional layer weights at the same 99% rate yields an overall sparsity of only 12% and accuracy of 86.9%. Simultaneously pruning both layer types to achieve 99% overall sparsity results in accuracy of 86.8% with 99% sparsity. These observations indicate that convolutional layers are the primary locus of critical weights for 3D feature extraction, and that heavy pruning of FC layers can dramatically reduce parameter count with limited or no loss in classification accuracy.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that convolutional layers are critical and FC layers can be heavily pruned is cleanly supported by the controlled ablation (H5), which provides direct evidence on PointNet. The uncertainty lies in generalization: P10 points out that the ablation was conducted only on PointNet, so the conclusion's extension to DGCNN and PointCNN (both labeled "PCNNs") is an extrapolation without direct empirical backing. The mechanistic insight from H5 (pruning FC improves accuracy) is so pronounced that it is likely a genuine property of PointNet, but DGCNN's graph convolution layers and PointCNN's X-transformation layers may distribute critical weights differently. The highlights (H5) are strong within the PointNet regime, but the single-architecture coverage means the conclusion's practical guidance—"aggressively compress FC layers in PCNNs"—must be applied cautiously to non-MLP architectures. The prior_probability of 0.7 reflects that the ablation's internal validity is high, while the external validity (generalization beyond PointNet) is unconfirmed but plausible given the common role of FC layers as classifiers across architectures.

nodes.title: Convolutional layers in PointNet retain critical weights after magnitude pruning while fully-connected layers are heavily pruned

nodes.content: Subnetworks extracted from overparameterized Point Cloud Neural Networks (PCNNs) at extreme sparsity (99% pruning) yield models with parameter counts far below several compact, hand-designed 3D architectures while achieving competitive accuracy on the ModelNet40 dataset. Specifically, pruned PointNet has 0.034M parameters and 87.1% accuracy; pruned DGCNN has 0.017M parameters and 86.3% accuracy; pruned PointCNN has 0.012M parameters and 85.4% accuracy. In comparison, compact hand-designed models such as PointCNN have 0.320M parameters and KCNet have 0.900M parameters. This shows that unstructured pruning of overparameterized PCNNs can produce extremely small models that are competitive with bespoke compact architectures.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that extremely pruned subnetworks can be smaller than compact hand-designed architectures while retaining "reasonable accuracy" is challenged by two load-bearing premises. P11 shows that the accuracy gap (5–8 points below the most accurate compact models, and below even the lowest-accuracy compact model at 88.9%) is substantial enough that "reasonable accuracy" is a misnomer for many practical thresholds: the pruned models are in a different accuracy regime. P12 shows a discrepancy of 0.2–0.8 points between the accuracy reported in Table 1 and Table 2 for the same model at the same sparsity without explanation, undermining the trustworthiness of the numbers. The highlight (H6) confirms that the parameter reduction is genuine and an order of magnitude below the smallest compact architectures, which is a real achievement. However, the interaction between the premises and the highlight is one of partial offsetting: H6 establishes the parameter benefit, but P11 establishes that the accuracy cost is higher than the conclusion's qualifiers suggest, and P12 introduces a measurement reliability risk. On balance, the conclusion is reliable for the claim that parameter counts can be dramatically reduced, but the claim of "competitive accuracy" is not supported given the gap to existing compact models. The prior_probability of 0.45 reflects this asymmetric support: parameter reduction is solid, accuracy competitiveness is not.

nodes.title: Extremely pruned PCNN subnetworks have lower parameter counts than compact hand-designed architectures with reasonable accuracy

nodes.content: In the iterative pruning procedure applied to Point Cloud Neural Network (PCNN) architectures (PointNet, DGCNN, PointCNN) for 3D point cloud classification, after each pruning round that removes the lowest-magnitude weights, the surviving weights are not reset to their original initialization values (no weight rewinding). The process only trains, prunes, and continues training from the surviving parameter values, deviating from the original Lottery Ticket Hypothesis protocol where the sparse subnetwork is rewound to the original initialization before retraining to isolate whether the subnetwork itself is trainable.Section 3, Figure 2, Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the procedure were changed to include weight rewinding to the original initialization (as in the canonical LTH experiment), the sparse subnetworks at 99% sparsity might not reach the reported accuracies (e.g., PointNet 86.3% on ModelNet40 via IMP, DGCNN 88.5%, PointCNN 87.4%). The observed performance could instead be an artifact of continued training on the same parameter trajectory, which would collapse the claim that these subnetworks are "winning tickets" trainable in isolation and reduce the result to a standard fine-tuning-based pruning outcome without the theoretical significance attributed to LTH in the conclusion's title and framing.
metadata.weakness_reason: The original LTH definition requires that the winning ticket be trainable from the original initialization when trained in isolation; rewinding is the standard method to test this. The paper’s procedure—training, pruning, and continuing without resetting—tests only whether continued fine-tuning of a pruned network preserves accuracy, not whether the sparse mask defines an independently trainable subnetwork. In the 2D pruning literature, networks pruned without rewinding often underperform when retrained from scratch, indicating that the retained accuracy may come from the fine-tuning trajectory rather than from the intrinsic structure of the subnetwork. The paper presents the subnetworks as LTH winning tickets but provides no evidence that they would achieve the same accuracy if trained from the original initialization with the sparse mask.

nodes.title: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis weight rewinding not implemented

nodes.content: All reported test accuracies for sparse subnetworks at 99% sparsity on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN (e.g., for subnetworks transferred from ShapeNetCore: PointNet with global Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) 86.3%, with one-shot global pruning 86.9%; DGCNN with IMP 88.5%, one-shot 88.0%; PointCNN with IMP 87.4%, one-shot 86.9%) are each based on a single experimental run. No error bars, standard deviations, or confidence intervals are reported, and no indication is given that multiple seeds or repetitions were averaged.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the accuracy values were found to vary by ±1–2 percentage points across seeds (a plausible range given the extreme sparsity and lack of regularization), the claimed “close to baseline” accuracy could break for some runs: for PointCNN, a 2.8-point gap could widen to 4–5 points, making the statement “close” ambiguous, and for DGCNN, the small 0.7-point advantage could disappear or reverse. The quantitative support for the existence of near-baseline sparse subnetworks would then be weaker than the single-run numbers suggest.
metadata.weakness_reason: Neural network pruning results, particularly at extreme sparsity levels (99%), are known to be sensitive to weight initialization, training stochasticity, and occasionally to the order of pruning steps. In the 2D LTH literature, reporting results over multiple seeds (typically 3–5) is standard practice to establish stability. Without such characterization, a single run’s outcome—especially a small gap of 0.5–2.8 percentage points from baseline—could be within the run-to-run noise. The paper provides no basis for discounting this possibility, leaving the reliability of the observed accuracy differential unquantified.

nodes.title: Single-run results without error bars

nodes.content: On the real-world scanned dataset ScanObjectNN, the 99%-sparse subnetworks transferred from ShapeNetCore produce test accuracies that are substantially lower than the dense baselines: PointNet drops from 68.2% to 64.7% (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP) or 62.7% (one-shot global pruning), DGCNN from 71.1% to 64.6% or 60.6%, and PointCNN from 70.4% to 65.3% or 59.3%. These drops of 3.5–10.1 percentage points are markedly larger than the corresponding drops on the synthetic ModelNet40 dataset (0.7–2.8 points).Table 1 (ScanObjectNN rows)

metadata.failure_mode: If the claim about near-baseline accuracy at 99% sparsity is intended to apply generally, the ScanObjectNN results refute it for real-world datasets: the drops of up to 10.1 points are not "close" by any reasonable threshold. The conclusion must be restricted to synthetic, clean datasets (ModelNet40). Without this restriction, a practitioner expecting similar behavior on real-world scans would be misled, and the conclusion's scope is materially narrower than stated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion claims that sparse subnetworks "produce test accuracies on standard 3D classification benchmarks that are close to the unpruned baselines." ScanObjectNN is a standard benchmark for real-world point cloud classification. The larger accuracy drops on this dataset indicate that the "close to baseline" property does not uniformly hold across all benchmarks; it is significantly weaker for real-world, noisy scans than for synthetic CAD data. The paper does not qualify the claim to exclude real-world data or explain why the drops occur, meaning the general statement is unsupported for this important data domain.

nodes.title: Larger accuracy drops on real-world ScanObjectNN

nodes.content: The performance comparison between global pruning (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP, and one-shot global pruning) and local pruning for PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN on ModelNet40 is presented via accuracy-vs-sparsity curves. These curves are plotted as single lines without any uncertainty bands, standard deviation shading, or indication that they were averaged over multiple runs or seeds. The claim that one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity exceeds all other methods evaluated relies on these single-trajectory curves.Figure 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the experiment were repeated with multiple seeds, the relative ordering of methods might shift: for instance, at 99% sparsity, a ±1% accuracy variation could make local pruning or IMP global outperform one-shot global on some seeds. The conclusion that one-shot global is the "best" strategy would then be unsupported, and the more modest claim that global methods tend to outperform local methods at extreme sparsity would remain plausible but not proven by the presented data.
metadata.weakness_reason: In pruning evaluation, differences between strategies can be small and subject to stochastic variation from training, pruning threshold choices, and data shuffling. Without uncertainty quantification, the observed ordering (global > local > baseline) may not be reproducible across different random seeds. The 2D pruning literature typically reports full curves with error bands; their absence here makes the comparison visually suggestive but statistically unanchored. The specific claim that one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity "exceeds all other methods evaluated" is the most aggressive comparative statement in the paper and should be supported by the strongest evidence, but it rests on a single curve without variance information.

nodes.title: No error bars or confidence intervals on pruning comparison curves

nodes.content: The local pruning method evaluated for PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN on ModelNet40 prunes the same percentage of weights from each layer independently, using a per-layer threshold. The global pruning methods (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP, and one-shot global pruning) are free to allocate pruning across layers arbitrarily, removing more weights from layers with lower-magnitude parameters. No ablation of local pruning under alternative per-layer ratios or variable pruning rates is performed, which might allow it to better match the layer importance distribution where convolutional layers are critical and fully-connected layers are less critical.Figure 2; Figure 3 (layerwise ablation)

metadata.failure_mode: If local pruning were given the flexibility to apply different sparsity ratios per layer (e.g., light pruning on conv, heavy on FC), its performance at extreme overall sparsity might match or approach that of global pruning. In that case, the conclusion that "global pruning (and one-shot) outperforms iterative local pruning" would be weakened to "the specific equal-ratio local pruning used here is worse than global pruning," which is a much narrower and less practically useful claim.
metadata.weakness_reason: A fixed per-layer equal-pruning-ratio strategy is known in the pruning literature to be suboptimal because different layers have different amounts of redundancy. The paper's own layerwise analysis (Conclusion 4, Figure 3) shows that convolutional layers are much more important than fully-connected layers in PCNNs. Using equal local ratios forces aggressive pruning of critical conv layers and insufficient pruning of redundant FC layers, potentially creating a systematically unfavorable comparison for the local method. The paper does not explore whether local pruning with layer-adaptive ratios would close the gap with global pruning, meaning the observed inferiority of local pruning could be an artifact of a poorly chosen local schedule rather than an inherent limitation.

nodes.title: Local pruning may be disadvantaged by equal per-layer pruning ratios

nodes.content: One-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity, tested on PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN with ModelNet40, exceeds all other methods evaluated, including global Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) which uses multiple iterative prune-retrain cycles. Since one-shot is equivalent to IMP with a single pruning cycle (J=1), the result that more iterative cycles produce worse performance at the same target sparsity is counterintuitive and is not explained or examined.Figure 2 caption

metadata.failure_mode: If the IMP schedule is tuned differently (e.g., smaller per-step pruning ratios, longer retraining between rounds, or learning rate rewarming), then the iterative method might recover or surpass one-shot performance at 99% sparsity. In that case, the paper's central comparative claim for Conclusion 2—that one-shot global pruning is the best strategy—would collapse to a statement about a specific, possibly suboptimal, configuration of IMP rather than a general property of pruning strategies for PCNNs.
metadata.weakness_reason: In standard LTH and pruning literature, iterative pruning with retraining typically finds better subnetworks than one-shot pruning, because the network can adapt between pruning rounds. The opposite result here suggests that the specific IMP schedule (20% per cycle, retraining for one cycle each iteration) may be suboptimal for PCNNs—for example, retraining for too few epochs may not recover from the damage, or the cumulative retraining after many cycles may overshoot. Without ablation of intermediate sparsity levels, different retraining lengths, or an explanation, the observed superiority of one-shot over IMP could be an artifact of a badly tuned IMP schedule rather than a reliable property of the pruning strategies for PCNNs.

nodes.title: One-shot outperforming IMP at 99% sparsity is unexpected and unexplained

nodes.content: When the sparse subnetworks discovered on ShapeNetCore are transferred to ScanObjectNN (a real-world scanned dataset) at 99% sparsity, the accuracies after fine-tuning are substantially lower than the baselines: PointNet 64.7% (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP) vs base 68.2% (−3.5 percentage points), DGCNN 64.6% (IMP) vs 71.1% (−6.5 pts), PointCNN 65.3% (IMP) vs 70.4% (−5.1 pts). One-shot global pruning variants show even larger drops (e.g., PointCNN 59.3% vs 70.4%, an 11.1-point drop).Table 1 (ScanObjectNN rows, 99% sparsity)

metadata.failure_mode: If a practitioner attempted to transfer a 99%-sparse subnetwork to a real-world point cloud classification task, the resulting accuracy would likely be substantially worse than expected from the unqualified claim of transferability. The conclusion is misleading unless explicitly restricted to ≤60% sparsity or to synthetic-to-synthetic transfer. Without such qualification, the claim of transferability is factually incorrect for the 99%-sparse real-data case.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion claims that winning-ticket subnetworks "transfer to smaller or different 3D datasets while retaining comparable or acceptable accuracy after fine-tuning." While the 60% sparsity transfers perform well (often exceeding baseline), the 99% transfers—which represent the extreme sparsity case emphasized in the paper—show accuracy drops that are large in absolute terms (3.5–11.1 points) and likely unacceptable for practical deployment on real-world data. The conclusion does not qualify this by sparsity level or domain type, so the unqualified claim of transferability is unsupported for the extreme sparsity regime on real-world scans.

nodes.title: Transfer to real-world ScanObjectNN at 99% sparsity shows large accuracy drops

nodes.content: The transfer experiment takes a sparse subnetwork discovered on ShapeNetCore and fine-tunes it on the target dataset (ModelNet40 or ScanObjectNN). There is no control experiment where a full dense model pre-trained on ShapeNetCore is fine-tuned on the target dataset and then pruned to the same sparsity post-hoc, or where the dense pre-trained model's weights are used directly without pruning, to determine whether the transferred accuracy is due to the sparsity pattern of the winning ticket or simply to the benefit of pre-training on a large dataset.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If a dense pre-trained model transferred from ShapeNetCore were found to achieve the same or better accuracies on ModelNet40/ScanObjectNN after fine-tuning (possibly when pruned to 99% sparsity post-transfer), then the sparsity pattern itself would contribute nothing to the transferability; the effect would be entirely due to pre-training. The conclusion that "winning tickets transfer" would be unsupported—what transfers is the pre-trained knowledge, and the sparsity is merely a compression method that preserves it to varying degrees.
metadata.weakness_reason: Transfer learning from a larger dataset to a smaller one is known to improve accuracy even without any pruning; the dense baselines reported (e.g., PointNet 87.5% on ModelNet40) are trained from scratch on ModelNet40 alone, not fine-tuned from ShapeNetCore pre-training. The observed improvements at 60% sparsity (e.g., PointNet 88.2% vs baseline 87.5%) could be entirely due to the additional ShapeNetCore pre-training, with the sparsity pattern providing no benefit or even slightly harming performance. Without a dense-transfer baseline, the paper cannot attribute the transfer results to the "winning ticket" property rather than to standard pre-training, undermining the specific claim that "winning tickets transfer."

nodes.title: No dense pre-training baseline to isolate sparsity benefit

nodes.content: The transfer experiments are all unidirectional: sparse subnetworks discovered on ShapeNetCore (the largest dataset used, with 51,300 instances across 55 categories) are transferred to ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN. No experiments test transfer from a smaller source to a larger target, between two synthetic datasets of comparable size, or from real (ScanObjectNN) to synthetic. Only one source dataset is used.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If winning tickets discovered on smaller or noisier datasets (e.g., ModelNet40 or ScanObjectNN) do not transfer to larger datasets or across different distribution shifts, the conclusion's general claim of transferability would be substantially narrower. A practitioner wanting to transfer a ticket from a custom small dataset could not rely on the paper's results, as those only cover the favorable case of a large, clean source.
metadata.weakness_reason: Transferability of winning tickets may depend on the source dataset's size and distribution. Demonstrating transfer from a large, clean, synthetic dataset to smaller datasets (including a noisy real-world one) is a useful first step, but it does not establish that the winning ticket property generalizes across arbitrary dataset pairs in the 3D domain. For instance, could a ticket found on ModelNet40 transfer to ShapeNetCore or to a different synthetic dataset like ScanNet? The paper does not address this. The claim of "transferability" is thus limited to a specific, perhaps favorable, source→target pairing.

nodes.title: Only one source dataset (ShapeNetCore) used

nodes.content: The ablation study separating convolutional layer pruning from fully-connected layer pruning was conducted only on the PointNet architecture. The claim that convolutional (feature-extraction) layers are critical and retain most important weights, whereas fully-connected layers can be heavily pruned, is generalized to Point Cloud Neural Networks (PCNNs) including DGCNN and PointCNN, despite no layerwise ablation being reported for those architectures.Figure 3 table (PointNet ablation)

metadata.failure_mode: If the same ablation were performed on DGCNN and PointCNN, it might reveal that fulcon layers in those architectures carry more critical weights (e.g., in PointCNN, the X-transformation layers mix spatial and channel information in a way that makes later FC layers less redundant). In that case, the conclusion's claim that FC layers can be "heavily pruned" across all PCNNs would be incorrect, and the practical guidance to prioritize conv preservation while aggressively eliminating FC parameters would lead to significant accuracy loss in non-MLP-based architectures.
metadata.weakness_reason: PointNet has a specific architecture: it uses shared MLPs for per-point feature extraction and a symmetric function for global feature aggregation. DGCNN uses graph convolutions with edge features, and PointCNN uses a learned X-transformation for convolution. These architectures have very different layer structures, and the distribution of critical weights across layer types could differ substantially. For example, in DGCNN, the graph convolution layers might behave differently from PointNet's MLPs, and the final FC layers might play a different role. Without replicating the conv vs FC ablation on at least one other architecture, the paper provides no evidence that the conclusion holds beyond PointNet.

nodes.title: Layerwise ablation performed only on PointNet architecture

nodes.content: On ModelNet40, the extremely pruned subnetworks achieve the following accuracies: PointNet 87.1%, DGCNN 86.3%, PointCNN 85.4%. The compact hand-designed architectures achieve accuracies from 88.9% (Spherical CNNs) to 93.8% (Point PN). The gap between the best pruned model (87.1%) and the best compact model (93.8%) is 6.7 percentage points; the gap to the lowest compact model (88.9%) is 1.8 points, but most compact models score above 90%.Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the threshold for "reasonable accuracy" is set at the level of the lowest compact model in the table (Spherical CNNs, 88.9%), the best pruned model (87.1%) does not meet it. A practitioner seeking an accurate compact model would prefer a compact architecture (e.g., PointCNN at 0.32M parameters and 92.2% accuracy) over a pruned subnetwork that is 10x smaller but 5 points less accurate. The conclusion therefore overstates the competitiveness of the pruned subnetworks: they are smaller but significantly less accurate, and the trade-off is not evaluated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion claims that the pruned subnetworks "reach parameter counts lower than some compact hand-designed PCNNs while retaining reasonable accuracy." The term "reasonable accuracy" is not quantified. A gap of 6.7 points (87.1% vs 93.8%) on a standard benchmark like ModelNet40 is practically significant for many applications; moreover, the compact models achieve these higher numbers at parameter budgets (0.32M–0.90M) that are still moderate. The pruned models' parameters are extremely low (0.012M–0.034M), but their accuracy is substantially below the range that the field considers competitive for ModelNet40 (state-of-the-art in 2024 is >94%). Without a shared accuracy threshold, the comparison lacks a basis for the "competitive" label.

nodes.title: Accuracy gap of 5–8 percentage points to compact architectures is substantial

nodes.content: Under transfer from ShapeNetCore, the 99%-sparse PointNet subnetwork accuracy on ModelNet40 is reported as 86.3% (global Iterative Magnitude Pruning, IMP) and 86.9% (one-shot global pruning). In a separate comparison of pruned models with compact architectures, a 99%-sparse PointNet subnetwork accuracy on ModelNet40 is reported as 87.1% without specifying the pruning strategy or whether transfer was used. The parameter count in both cases is 0.034M (1% of the original 3.4M), suggesting the same sparsity. The source of the 0.2–0.8 percentage point discrepancy is not explained, and it is not clarified whether the comparison table uses the same transfer protocol or a different experimental setup.Table 1 (PointNet 99% rows), Table 2 (PointNet row)

metadata.failure_mode: If the inconsistent numbers reflect unrecognized experimental variability (e.g., different seeds produce accuracies fluctuating over a 1-point range), then the specific accuracy values in Table 2 (e.g., 87.1%) are not reliable point estimates for comparing against compact models. A reader trying to decide whether to use a pruned subnetwork over a compact architecture cannot determine which accuracy number is credible. The comparative claim of "competitive accuracy" would be weakened because the reference number for the pruned model is uncertain.
metadata.weakness_reason: Reproducibility is a core expectation in pruning research. The discrepancies between Table 1 (IMP 86.3%, one-shot 86.9%) and Table 2 (87.1%) for the same model at the same sparsity on the same dataset, without explanation of which pruning method or transfer protocol was used, undermines confidence that the numbers are stable and consistently obtained. Possible causes include different training seeds, different pruning strategies not identified, or test set variability. Without clarification, the reader cannot trust the accuracy values as reliable evidence for the parameter-efficiency comparison in Table 2.

nodes.title: Inconsistent accuracy numbers for same model and sparsity across tables

nodes.content: The existence of magnitude-based sparse subnetworks approaching dense baseline accuracy is demonstrated across three fundamentally different PCNN architectures: PointNet (pointwise MLP, per-point feature extraction with max-pooling aggregation), DGCNN (graph convolution on dynamic nearest-neighbor graphs), and PointCNN (convolution with learned X-transformation for spatial feature ordering). On ModelNet40, at 99% sparsity via transferred IMP, the accuracies are 86.3% (PointNet), 88.5% (DGCNN), and 87.4% (PointCNN), each within 0.7–2.8 points of their respective dense baselines (87.5%, 89.2%, 90.2%).

metadata.credit: The variety of architectures tested guards against the risk that the finding is an artifact of a single model design (e.g., only pointwise MLP or only graph convolution). Without this breadth, the conclusion would be restricted to one paradigm and the claim that "PCNNs" contain sparse subnetworks would be unsupported for important architecture families. By covering all three major PCNN design approaches, the highlight underwrites the generalization of the conclusion across the PCNN landscape, giving practitioners confidence that the phenomenon is likely to hold for other point cloud networks within these paradigms.

nodes.title: Evaluation across three diverse PCNN architectures

nodes.content: A controlled ablation on PointNet (Figure 3 table) directly tests the effect of pruning both conv and FC layers to 99% on ModelNet40, yielding a model with 99% overall sparsity (0.034M parameters) and test accuracy 86.8%, compared to the unpruned baseline of 87.5%. This experiment is conducted on the target dataset itself (no transfer confound), and includes three comparators: prune-only-FC (87% sparsity, 88.3% acc), prune-only-conv (12% sparsity, 86.9% acc), and no pruning (0% sparsity, 87.5% acc).

metadata.credit: This ablation provides the cleanest evidence for the core claim: under a direct, within-dataset evaluation, a 99%-sparse PointNet subnetwork achieves accuracy within 0.7 points of the dense baseline. It rules out the concern that the transferred-table results (Table 1) might be confounded by the pre-training/fine-tuning protocol or by dataset-specific artifacts of ShapeNetCore. Without this direct test, the quantitative claim of near-baseline accuracy at 99% sparsity would rest entirely on transfer results, which the paper acknowledges involve an additional fine-tuning step that could introduce biasing effects. This highlight gives the conclusion a solid empirical anchor on the target benchmark itself.

nodes.title: Direct ablation control on PointNet confirms sparse subnetwork accuracy

nodes.content: The finding that global pruning (IMP and one-shot) outperforms local pruning at extreme sparsity (Figure 2) is independently corroborated by the layerwise analysis (Figure 3), which shows that convolutional layers carry most critical weights while FC layers are largely redundant. Global pruning can naturally allocate sparsity unevenly, preserving conv layers and heavily pruning FC layers, whereas local pruning with equal per-layer ratios would apply the same aggressive removal to critical conv layers. The ablation data (prune-only-FC yields 88.3% accuracy, prune-only-conv yields 86.9%, both at 99% internal rate) confirm this mechanistic logic.

metadata.credit: This cross-validation preempts the concern that the global-versus-local comparison in Figure 2 might be an artifact of the specific pruning schedule or hyperparameters (addressed as a potential weak point). The independent layerwise evidence provides a mechanistic explanation for why global pruning should work better: it matches the natural distribution of critical weights across layers. Without this corroboration, the superiority claim would rest solely on the single-run curves of Figure 2. The layerwise analysis raises the credibility of the comparative claim from an observation to a structurally grounded finding about PCNN architecture.

nodes.title: Cross-validation between global pruning superiority and layerwise criticality

nodes.content: At 60% sparsity, the subnetworks discovered on ShapeNetCore and transferred to ModelNet40 (synthetic) and ScanObjectNN (real scans) achieve accuracies that meet or exceed the baselines trained from scratch on the target datasets: on ModelNet40, PointNet reaches 88.2% (IMP) vs base 87.5%, DGCNN 90.1% vs 89.2%, PointCNN 90.6% vs 90.2%; on ScanObjectNN, PointNet reaches 71.7% (IMP) vs base 68.2%, DGCNN 75.2% vs 71.1%, PointCNN 73.2% vs 70.4%. All three models across both datasets show improved or near-identical accuracy at 60% sparsity.

metadata.credit: This result preempts the concern that the reported transferability only works on synthetic data or for a single architecture. By showing consistent accuracy at or above the baseline on a real-world, noisy dataset (ScanObjectNN) across all three architecture families, the highlight supports the claim that the subnetworks capture features that are genuinely transferable across domain shifts—at least at moderate sparsity. Without this demonstration on real data, the transfer claim would be limited to the synthetic-to-synthetic case, which is less demanding. The real-data results give the transferability conclusion practical weight for deployment scenarios.

nodes.title: Successful transfer to both synthetic and real-world datasets at 60% sparsity

nodes.content: The ablation study on PointNet (Figure 3 table) systematically separates the effect of pruning convolutional layers and fully-connected layers by pruning each type alone at 99% internal sparsity, while keeping the other type intact, and comparing to the unpruned baseline and to joint pruning. The results: prune-FC-only yields 87% overall sparsity and accuracy 88.3% (higher than baseline 87.5%); prune-conv-only yields 12% overall sparsity and accuracy 86.9%; prune-both yields 99% sparsity and accuracy 86.8%. This 2×2 design isolates the contribution of each layer type to accuracy and parameter savings.

metadata.credit: This controlled design provides direct evidence that FC layers can be almost entirely removed without harming accuracy (even improving it), while conv layers are necessary for retaining performance. It preempts the alternative explanation that the criticality of conv layers is merely an artifact of their larger size or different learning rate. The comparison of prune-only-FC (improved accuracy) vs prune-only-conv (degraded accuracy) makes the causal claim that conv layers carry essential geometric features while FC layers are dispensable. Without this ablation, the conclusion would rely on weight-magnitude distributions alone, which are correlational. The highlight underwrites a mechanistic attribution for the layerwise importance claim.

nodes.title: Controlled conv vs FC ablation isolates layer criticality

nodes.content: Table 2 lists five compact 3D architectures (PointCNN 0.320M, Spherical CNNs 0.500M, Dense Point 0.530M, KCNet 0.900M, Point PN 0.800M) alongside the pruned subnetworks' parameter counts (PointNet 0.034M, DGCNN 0.017M, PointCNN 0.012M) on the same ModelNet40 classification benchmark. The pruned models have 10–75× fewer parameters than the smallest compact architecture listed (PointCNN 0.320M). The accuracy numbers for the compact models are sourced from their original publications, providing an objective external reference.

metadata.credit: By situating the pruned models against a published set of low-parameter alternatives, the paper provides an external reference point that is not available from the pruning experiments alone. Without this comparison, the claim of "extremely small" would be self-referential. The highlight preempts the concern that moderate parameter counts can already be achieved with careful architecture design: the pruned models are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than many such designs, a difference that cannot be dismissed as within the margin of noise. Even with the accuracy gap noted separately, this parameter reduction is a concrete quantitative achievement that gives the conclusion its practical significance—extremely low-resource deployment becomes feasible.

nodes.title: Direct parameter-count comparison with published compact architectures

steps.reasoning: State the upstream result used as starting point: one-shot global magnitude pruning and global IMP are effective pruning strategies for PCNNs at extreme sparsity levels, and these strategies identify winning-ticket subnetworks that preserve accuracy at high pruning rates (this is conclusion 2 treated as known for this derivation).

Reiterate the experimental objective: to find sparse subnetworks $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with high sparsity (e.g., 99% sparsity means $p=99\%$ of weights are removed and only the top $100-p=1\%$ of weights by magnitude remain) whose test accuracy $d'$ on downstream tasks is close to the dense baseline accuracy $a$.

Describe the experimental measurement and reporting format used to substantiate the existence claim: the authors present quantitative test accuracies on the ModelNet40 dataset for three PCNN architectures (PointNet, DGCNN, PointCNN) after applying either iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) or one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity; the numerical results are provided in the transfer table reported as "Table 1" where pruned-model accuracies are listed alongside the respective dense baselines.
Table 1

Extract and state the reported Base (dense) accuracies on ModelNet40 as given by the authors: PointNet base accuracy is 87.5%; DGCNN base accuracy is 89.2%; PointCNN base accuracy is 90.2%. These baseline numbers are the reference points used to judge how close pruned-subnetwork accuracies are to the unpruned models.
Table 1

Extract and state the reported pruned-subnetwork accuracies at 99% sparsity transferred from ShapeNetCore to ModelNet40 as reported in the same table: for PointNet the IMP result is 86.3% and the one-shot global pruning result is 86.9%; for DGCNN the IMP result is 88.5% and the one-shot result is 88.0%; for PointCNN the IMP result is 87.4% and the one-shot result is 86.9%. Present these numbers as the empirical evidence that retaining only the top 1% of weights preserves the majority of classification performance on ModelNet40 for these architectures.
Table 1

Compare each pruned result to its dense baseline numerically and state the margin of degradation (where applicable): 
- PointNet: baseline 87.5% → IMP 86.3% (drop 1.2 percentage points) and one-shot 86.9% (drop 0.6 percentage points). 
- DGCNN: baseline 89.2% → IMP 88.5% (drop 0.7 percentage points) and one-shot 88.0% (drop 1.2 percentage points). 
- PointCNN: baseline 90.2% → IMP 87.4% (drop 2.8 percentage points) and one-shot 86.9% (drop 3.3 percentage points). 
These small absolute declines indicate that the pruned subnetworks achieve test accuracies close to the unpruned baselines on ModelNet40.
Table 1

Synthesize the formal and empirical items: given the LTH framework and pruning mechanics (mask $\mathbf{m}$ selecting the top-magnitude weights) and given the reported empirical accuracies at 99% sparsity (retaining 1% of weights) that are near the dense baselines for PointNet, DGCNN, and PointCNN, conclude that PCNNs contain highly sparse, trainable subnetworks ("winning tickets") up to 99% sparsity whose retained weights produce test accuracies on standard 3D classification benchmarks that are close to the unpruned baselines.
Table 1

Define PCNN as "Point Cloud Neural Networks", i.e., neural network architectures that operate on 3D point cloud data; define sparsity as the fraction of weights set to zero expressed in percent (for example, "99% sparsity" means 99% of the original weights have been removed and 1% remain).

State the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) formalism used: a dense network is $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$; a binary mask is $\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$; a sparse subnetwork is $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta})$. The LTH seeks $\mathbf{m}$ such that the sparse subnetwork trained in isolation matches or exceeds the dense network accuracy. Include this LTH attribution as presented.
[17]

Formalize the pruning procedures compared: define iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) as the repeated process where at each round $j$ the network $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{m}^{(j-1)}\odot\theta^{(j-1)})$ is trained, a threshold $\alpha^{(j)}$ is chosen, and the mask is updated by setting $m_{l}^{(j)}[i]=0$ for weights with $|\theta_{l}^{(j-1)}[i]|\leq\alpha^{(j)}$; define one-shot (single-step) pruning as the special case with number of pruning rounds $J=1$. Explicitly note that the global threshold $\alpha^{(j)}$ is determined by the $(1-p)^{th}$ percentile of the magnitudes of all weights across all layers for a desired pruning percentage $p$, while local (layer-wise) thresholds $\alpha_{l}^{(j)}$ are determined by the $(1-p)^{th}$ percentile of magnitudes within layer $l$.
[65]

Clarify the distinction: "global magnitude pruning" means applying a single global threshold across all layers (so the smallest-magnitude weights across the whole network are pruned first); "iterative local (layer-wise) pruning" means each layer prunes according to its own threshold independently. State that one-shot global pruning corresponds to the one-step ($J=1$) application of the global threshold.

Describe the experimental protocol that supports the empirical comparison: the authors applied IMP (global), global one-shot pruning, and local iterative pruning across three PCNN architectures (PointNet, DGCNN, PointCNN) and datasets (ModelNet40, ScanObjectNN, ShapeNetCore), using train-prune-rewind cycles with model-specific numbers of cycles (e.g., 100 cycles for PointNet, 80 cycles for DGCNN, 80 cycles for PointCNN) and standard optimizers and hyperparameters reported in the experiments section; these setups produced the performance curves compared in the paper.

Present the empirical evidence from the paper comparing pruning strategies: the paper reports that global pruning methods (both global IMP and one-shot global magnitude pruning) maintain higher accuracy at extreme sparsity levels than iterative local pruning; specifically, the paper states that "Global pruning methods are more effective in identifying winning tickets at extreme sparsity levels than iterative pruning methods relying on local pruning criteria" and that "one-shot global pruning at 99% sparsity exceeds all other methods evaluated." Use the aggregated performance visualization and method comparisons described by the authors as the experimental basis for this claim.
Figure 2

Conclude from the formal definitions and the reported experiments that global magnitude pruning, whether executed as a single-shot operation ($J=1$) or as global IMP (multiple rounds with a global threshold), is an effective pruning strategy for PCNNs and empirically outperforms iterative local pruning at extreme sparsity levels in the authors' experiments; treat the reported Figure 2 performance curves and associated textual claims as the primary empirical support for this conclusion.
Figure 2

State upstream results used as starting points: (a) one-shot global magnitude pruning and global IMP are effective pruning strategies for PCNNs at extreme sparsity levels (conclusion 2), and (b) PCNNs contain highly sparse trainable subnetworks up to 99% sparsity whose retained weights preserve near-baseline accuracy (conclusion 1). Treat these two conclusions as established facts for the purpose of the transferability derivation.

Define the transfer procedure formally as used by the authors in the transferability section: let $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ be two datasets with different distributions; let $\mathcal{F}_{1}(\mathbf{x};\theta_{1})$ be a network trained on $D_{1}$ and a sparse mask $\mathbf{m}_{1}\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta_{1}|}$ be obtained from $\mathcal{F}_{1}$ by pruning; initialize $\mathcal{F}_{2}(\mathbf{x};\theta_{2})$ with $\theta_{2}=\mathbf{m}_{1}\odot\theta_{1}$ (i.e., keep only the weights retained by $\mathbf{m}_{1}$) and then fine-tune $\mathcal{F}_{2}$ on $D_{2}$. The transferability condition considered by the authors is that the fine-tuned sparse model attains accuracy $a_{2}^{\prime}\approx a_{2}$ where $a_{2}$ is the baseline accuracy of a dense model trained on $D_{2}$.

Describe the experimental setup used to test transferability: the authors obtain sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) from models trained on the larger ShapeNetCore dataset and transfer those sparse masks and weights to models trained and fine-tuned on smaller or different datasets (ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN); performance after fine-tuning on the target datasets is reported in Table 1 to quantify transfer success.
Table 1

Present the reported transferred results for 60% sparsity (i.e., retaining 40% of weights) from ShapeNetCore to ModelNet40 as given in Table 1, including the dense baselines for comparison: 
- PointNet: dense baseline on ModelNet40 is 87.5% → transferred 60% IMP result 88.2% and one-shot 87.8% (both are comparable to or slightly better than the baseline). 
- DGCNN: baseline 89.2% → transferred 60% IMP 90.1% and one-shot 90.4% (both exceed the baseline). 
- PointCNN: baseline 90.2% → transferred 60% IMP 90.6% and one-shot 90.4% (both slightly exceed the baseline). 
These numbers indicate that sparse subnetworks discovered on ShapeNetCore can be fine-tuned on ModelNet40 to achieve performance comparable to or better than dense baselines.
Table 1

Present the reported transferred results to ScanObjectNN for the 60% sparsity case (as given in Table 1) to show behavior on a different, real-world dataset: for PointNet the dense baseline on ScanObjectNN is 68.2% while the transferred 60% IMP ticket yields 71.7% and the transferred one-shot yields 70.5%; for DGCNN the transferred 60% IMP yields 75.2% and one-shot 74.9% versus baseline 71.1%; for PointCNN transferred 60% IMP yields 73.2% and one-shot 72.9% versus baseline 70.4%. These entries demonstrate that transfer performance can be comparable or even improve over baseline on the real-world ScanObjectNN dataset in the reported experiments.
Table 1

Explain how the transfer results support the claim: the transfer experiments use masks $\mathbf{m}_1$ obtained on a larger dataset $D_{1}=$ ShapeNetCore and initialize/fine-tune models on $D_{2}=$ ModelNet40 or ScanObjectNN using $\theta_{2}=\mathbf{m}_{1}\odot\theta_{1}$; because the fine-tuned sparse networks achieve accuracies $a_{2}^{\prime}$ that are comparable to or better than the dense baselines $a_{2}$ (as quantified in the previous steps), the authors conclude that winning tickets discovered on one 3D domain can be reused to reduce training and parameter costs on related 3D classification tasks.
[5]

Synthesize: starting from the established effectiveness of global pruning (conclusion 2) and the existence of highly sparse accurate subnetworks (conclusion 1), and given the formal transfer procedure and the empirical results in Table 1 showing transferred sparse models achieving comparable or acceptable accuracy on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN, conclude that winning-ticket subnetworks discovered on a larger 3D dataset transfer to smaller or different 3D datasets while retaining comparable accuracy after fine-tuning.
Table 1

Start from the upstream known fact: PCNNs contain highly sparse, trainable subnetworks up to 99% sparsity that preserve near-baseline accuracy (conclusion 1); treat that result as established for this analysis of layer-wise importance.

Define the layer types referenced: "Conv" denotes convolutional layers responsible for feature extraction in the PCNN architectures (including architectures termed "conv" or point-convolutional components), and "FC" denotes fully connected layers (dense layers, typically at the end of the network used for classification). Define "pruning only FC" to mean applying the pruning procedure to FC layers only while leaving conv layers unpruned; similarly "pruning only conv" means pruning conv layers only.

Describe the ablation protocol used by the authors: they applied 99% pruning targeted to only FC layers, only conv layers, and to both, and they report the resulting overall sparsity (fraction of weights removed across the whole network) and the test accuracy on ModelNet40 for PointNet in the Table reproduced as part of Figure 3.
Figure 3

State the concrete ablation numbers reported in the Figure 3 table (for PointNet): 
- No pruning (Conv not pruned, FC not pruned): pruning(%) = 0, sparsity(%) = 0, accuracy = 87.5% (dense baseline). 
- Prune only Conv (Conv pruned ✓, FC not pruned ×) with 99% pruning applied produces net sparsity 12% and accuracy 86.9%. 
- Prune only FC (Conv not pruned ×, FC pruned ✓) with 99% pruning applied produces net sparsity 87% and accuracy 88.3%. 
- Prune both Conv and FC (both ✓) with 99% pruning applied produces net sparsity 99% and accuracy 86.8%.
Figure 3

Interpret the ablation numbers: pruning only FC layers at an aggressive 99% per-layer pruning results in a high overall sparsity (87% of weights removed globally) while improving accuracy to 88.3% compared to the dense baseline 87.5%, indicating that many FC-layer parameters were removable and that removing them did not harm and may even help generalization. Conversely, pruning only conv layers at 99% per-layer pruning produced only 12% net sparsity (implying that conv-layer magnitudes were generally larger and thus fewer conv weights met the pruning threshold) and decreased accuracy to 86.9%, indicating that conv layers contain many of the task-critical, high-magnitude weights.

Combine experimental evidence with the LTH magnitude-pruning mechanism: because magnitude-based pruning removes small-magnitude weights and preserves high-magnitude weights, the observation that FC pruning removes many weights while conv pruning removes few weights implies that high-magnitude (therefore task-critical) weights are concentrated in conv layers, whereas FC layers harbor many low-magnitude, removable parameters. The authors explicitly state that convolutional layers preserve most of the weights under IMP and that FC layers contribute most of the removable parameters; treat this textual statement and the ablation table as the justification.
Figure 3

Conclude that layer-wise importance analysis shows convolutional (feature-extraction) layers are critical and retain most important weights after magnitude pruning, while fully-connected layers can be heavily pruned to dramatically reduce parameter count with limited or no loss in classification accuracy, using the PointNet ablation as the empirical example supporting this claim.
Figure 3

Start from the upstream known result: PCNNs contain highly sparse subnetworks (conclusion 1); this established ability to extract very sparse, accurate subnetworks is the basis for comparing pruned parameter counts to those of compact hand-designed PCNNs.

Describe the comparative evaluation presented by the authors: the paper compiles a table (Table 2) listing parameter counts (in millions, "Param (M)") and ModelNet40 accuracies for existing less-parametric PCNN models (hand-designed compact architectures) and for the authors' extremely pruned subnetworks derived from overparameterized models; these numbers provide the basis for a direct comparison of parameter budget versus accuracy.
Table 2

Extract the specific parameter-accuracy entries from Table 2 for the authors' pruned subnetworks on ModelNet40: 
- Ours (PointNet): Param = 0.034M, Accuracy = 87.1%. 
- Ours (DGCNN): Param = 0.017M, Accuracy = 86.3%. 
- Ours (PointCNN): Param = 0.012M, Accuracy = 85.4%.
Also extract a few representative compact model entries from the same table for contrast: PointCNN (hand-designed) Param = 0.320M, Accuracy = 92.2%; KCNet Param = 0.900M, Accuracy = 91.0%.
Table 2

Compare parameter budgets explicitly: the pruned PointNet at 0.034M parameters is approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the compact PointCNN at 0.320M parameters and far smaller than KCNet at 0.900M parameters; similarly, pruned DGCNN (0.017M) and pruned PointCNN (0.012M) are substantially smaller than the hand-designed compact models listed.
Table 2

Assess accuracy trade-offs reported: although some hand-designed compact models report higher absolute accuracy (for example, PointCNN 92.2% at 0.320M), the pruned subnetworks achieve competitive accuracies given their much smaller parameter budgets (for example, pruned PointNet 87.1% at 0.034M, pruned DGCNN 86.3% at 0.017M, pruned PointCNN 85.4% at 0.012M). The authors summarize that the pruned extremely-small models perform similarly to other less-parameter models, emphasizing the trade-off between parameter count and absolute accuracy.
Table 2

Conclude that unstructured magnitude pruning of overparameterized PCNNs can produce extremely small models whose parameter counts are substantially lower than some compact, hand-designed PCNNs, while retaining reasonable and in some cases competitive accuracy on ModelNet40, supporting the assertion that extremely pruned PCNN subnetworks can reach parameter counts lower than several compact architectures while maintaining acceptable performance.
Table 2

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges several scientifically meaningful unresolved issues and limitations that remain after the reported empirical findings: (1) theoretical understanding: there is no formal proof within this work that explains why LTH-style sparse winning tickets exist specifically for PCNN architectures and how geometric invariances and structural constraints (rotations, scalings, part relationships) are preserved by magnitude-based pruning; (2) invariance and structural-preservation guarantees: the degree to which pruning preserves exact geometric invariances or structural semantics of 3D shapes is not proven and remains to be quantified formally beyond observed empirical robustness; (3) computational cost and practicality: identifying winning tickets via iterative pruning and retraining is computationally expensive for each task/dataset, and the development or validation of cheaper single-pass or more efficient algorithms tailored to 3D models is an open engineering challenge; (4) transfer robustness and domain gaps: while transferred tickets showed good results in some cases, transfers to real-world scanned datasets (e.g., ScanObjectNN) exhibited larger accuracy drops than synthetic-to-synthetic transfers, leaving open the limits of ticket transferability across domain shifts and noisy real-world data; (5) runtime and hardware acceleration implications: because unstructured sparsity does not automatically translate to proportional inference speedups on all hardware, quantifying actual latency, energy, and memory benefits of these extremely sparse PCNN subnetworks on edge and accelerator platforms remains an open empirical question for practical deployment.
